query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A brief high‐temperature annealing treatment of FeNiCrCoCu coatings facilitates controlled oxidation and near‐surface grain refinement, leading to the formation of a uniform, protective oxide tribolayer and a hardened microstructure that together enhance wear resistance and reduce plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a short annealing treatment at 600–700 °C post-deposition.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed at high temperatures (600–700 °C) under identical loads and sliding speeds for both annealed and as-deposited coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The annealing treatment promotes the formation of a continuous oxide tribofilm and refines the near-surface grain structure.
generation.mechanism: Post-deposition annealing accelerates controlled oxidation at the surface that forms a continuous and stable oxide layer, while also inducing recrystallization that leads to a finer, harder microstructure. This dual change mitigates direct metal-to-metal contact, reduces dislocation movement and plastic deformation, and thus lowers the overall wear rate during high-temperature sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed coatings will exhibit lower specific wear rates, a more continuous and thicker protective oxide film, increased surface hardness, and fewer signs of severe plastic deformation in cross-sectional microstructural analyses.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any post-deposition heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (600–700 °C) at controlled loads and speeds; different temperature regimes (e.g., room temperature) or sliding conditions might not exhibit the same benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the relative contributions of the oxide tribofilm formation versus grain refinement in improving wear resistance, and the optimal annealing duration and temperature to maximize these effects remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same conventional metal substrate. Apply a brief annealing treatment at 600–700 °C to one set while leaving the other set as-deposited. Conduct pin-on-disc sliding tests at 600–700 °C under the same load and sliding speed. Characterize both sets for wear rate, friction coefficient, oxide film formation (using SEM/EDS), and near-surface microstructural features (via cross-sectional microscopy and nanoindentation).
measurements: Continuity and thickness of the oxide tribolayer (SEM/EDS)
Grain size and hardness (nanoindentation and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coatings do not display statistically significant improvements in wear resistance (i.e., similar or higher wear rates, comparable or less continuous oxide layers, and unchanged hardness or microstructural refinement) compared to the as-deposited coatings under identical high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

In order to determine whether there was oxidation wear in the wear process, the EDS analysis was carried out for the wear debris A and wear scars B, C, D, and E of the coating samples, as shown in Figure 12b–e. The element contents at A–E are illustrated in Figure 12f–j, and clearly, there was oxidation wear at all points A–E. During the oxidation wear, the oxidation film generated was ductile and softer than the substrate. Under the shear force between the friction pair, partial oxidation films would be exfoliated, and the exfoliated films could be smeared on the sample surface, serving as a solid lubricant and thereby reducing wear []. As shown in Figure 12f,g, the O element content of wear debris A was obviously higher than that at B without wear debris, which confirmed that the oxidation film was continuously exfoliated to form wear debris. In Figure 12g–j, the O element content at D and E was much higher than that at B and C, respectively, suggesting that the oxidation wear of the UB-treated coatings was more obvious. This is because the grain refinement, dislocation, and high internal stress generated from the UB treatment could make the oxidation film denser and thicker [].

The fine-grained sample has higher surface hardness and mechanical strength, which is helpful to improve the wear resistance []. Compared with other materials, this can give us some inspiration for later work. The average wear rate of TiO2 10 wt.% NiAl coating deposited on the low alloy steel 40Cr4 surface is 9.821 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1, and the wear rate of TiO213 wt.% NiAl coating 40Cr4 is 1.22 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the normal load of 10 N and sliding speed of 500 mm/s [], which is close to that of FG HEA under the load of 30 N and sliding speed of 5 mm/s. The wear rate of AlCrSiN-coated tool steel K340 is 5.681 × 10−7 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the load of 10 N and 10 cm/s []. The average wear rate of AlTiSiN + TiSiN coatings deposited on the H 13 tool steels is 2.30 × 10−8 and 1.31 × 10−8 mm3 N−1 m−1 for normal load of 30 and 50 N at the lubricated conditions, respectively []. Tubrication can effectively improve the wear resistance of materials, which presents good inspiration for our later work.

decision.trend: Early studies (PMC5461481) examined the structural stability of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) under extreme temperatures and pressures, noting the role of phase transitions (fcc ↔ hcp) in CoCrFeMnNi-type systems. Subsequent work (PMC7512501) showed that a related Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi HEA coating improves wear resistance on Mg substrates and that microstructural evolution (e.g., presence of second phases, grain refinement) strongly affects wear mechanisms. Later, investigations of friction and wear in CoCrFeMnNi alloys in controlled environments (PMC7311485) revealed low friction coefficients linked to dynamically formed refined grains in the wear track, highlighting the importance of deformation-induced structure changes. Most recently, high-temperature testing of FeCoNiMnCu coatings on steel (PMC10908794) demonstrated that protective oxide or spinel layers can develop in service, leading to improved wear resistance and hardness at elevated temperatures. Despite these advances, the specific controlling mechanisms governing wear and microscopic deformation in FeNiCrCoCu coatings under high-temperature sliding remain unresolved, including how dynamic oxidation, short-range ordering, and local stress-driven phase changes interplay to determine tribological behavior.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how oxidation-driven tribofilm formation, local chemical ordering, and high-temperature phase stability together dictate the wear resistance and plasticity mechanisms of FeNiCrCoCu coatings during sliding. While various studies highlight hardness increases, oxide-layer formation, and dynamic grain refinement, no single mechanistic framework has unified these observations under elevated-temperature sliding conditions for FeNiCrCoCu.
decision.lever: Vary the post-deposition heat treatment (e.g., a short high-temperature annealing at 600–700 °C vs. no anneal) for identically deposited FeNiCrCoCu coatings and systematically assess oxide-scale formation, microstructure evolution, wear loss, surface hardness, and deformation substructures under pin-on-disc testing at 600–700 °C. Compare the annealed vs. as-deposited states under identical sliding loads and speeds, then measure changes in wear rate and near-surface dislocation substructure via cross-sectional microscopy.
decision.why: Based on prior findings that dynamic oxidation and microstructural evolution (grain refinement, oxide/spinel tribofilms) can stabilize wear properties at elevated temperatures for CoCrFeNi(Mn, Cu) alloys, scrutinizing whether a deliberate annealing step can promote or alter the formation of stable protective oxide films and refined near-surface microstructures is the most direct way to isolate their role. If post-annealed coatings do not exhibit enhanced wear resistance or refined dislocation structures under the same high-temperature sliding conditions, it would falsify the hypothesis that thermally mediated changes in oxide-layer evolution and microstructure control the wear-deformation response.
